tasks.title: CCD Image Processing
tasks.statement:
As an exercise of image processing, this problem involves use of a simple calculator and tabular data (table 1.1) which contains the pixel values of an image during the given exposure time. This image, which is a part of a larger CCD image, was taken by a small CCD camera, installed on an amateur telescope and using a V band filter. Figure 1.1 shows this pixels image that contains 5 stars.

In table 1.1 the first row and column indicates the pixels’ x and y coordinates. Table 1.2 gives the telescope and the image specifications.

The observer identified stars 1, 3 and 4 by comparing this image with standard star catalogues. Table 1.3 shows stars true magnitudes as given in the catalogue.

parts.question: Using the available data, determine the instrumental magnitudes of the stars in the image. Assume the dark current is negligible and the image is flat fielded. For simplicity you can use a square aperture. Hint: The instrumental magnitude is calculated using the difference between the measured flux from the star in the aperture and the flux from an equivalent area of dark sky.
parts.reference: To measure instrumental magnitude we should choose an aperture. Careful investigation of the image, shows that a 5 × 5 pixel aperture is enough to measure m_inst for all stars. m_inst can be calculated using the given formula. Star 1: -3.02, Star 3: -5.85, Star 4: -4.04.

parts.question: The instrumental magnitude of a star in a CCD image is related to true magnitude... Calculate the zero point constant for identified stars. Calculate average zero point constant. Hint: Zero point constant is the constant reducing extinction-free magnitudes to the true magnitude.
Calculate true magnitudes of stars 2 and 5.
parts.reference: Following part (a) for stars 2 and 5, we can calculate true magnitudes (m_true) for these stars. Star 2: 9.93, Star 5: 11.4

parts.question: Calculate CCD pixel scale for the CCD camera in units of arcsec.
Calculate average brightness of dark sky in magnitude per square arcsec.
Use a suitable plot to estimate astronomical seeing in arcsec.
parts.reference: To estimate astronomical seeing, first we plot pixel values in x or y direction for one of the bright stars in the image. The FWHM of pixel values is 1 pixel, hence astronomical seeing is equal to 4.3 arcsec.

tasks.title: Venus
tasks.statement: An observer in Deh-Namak (you will be taking the observational part of the exam in this region tonight) has observed Venus for seven months, started from September 2008 and continued until March 2009. During the observation, a research CCD camera and an image processing software were used to take high resolution images and to extract high precision data. Table 2.1 shows the collected data during the observation.

parts.question: Using given data in table 2.1, calculate the Sun-Venus-Earth angle SVE. This is angular separation between the Sun and the Earth as seen from Venus. Write angle in column 2 of Table 2.2 in your answer sheet for the all observing dates. Hint: Remember that the line between light and shadow, in the phases, is an ellipse arc.
parts.reference: Phase formula and calculation of SVE angles for all dates as presented in Table 2.2.

parts.question: Calculate Sun – Venus distance in AU and write it down in column 3 of table 2.2 for all observation dates.
parts.reference: Sine rule application using Earth-Sun distance, elongation, and SVE angle to find Sun-Venus distance for all observation dates.

parts.question: Plot Sun – Venus distance versus observing date.
parts.reference: Plot of Sun-Venus distance versus observing date.

parts.question: Find perihelion and aphelion distances of Venus from the Sun.
Calculate semi-major axis a of the Venus orbit.
Calculate eccentricity e of Venus orbit.
